summary: An experimental proposal for a company-name-to-URL mapping service built on whois, one of the oldest and simplest Internet directory protocols. It explores whether a very simple, widely deployed protocol can succeed where more complex ones have not.

eli5.summary: Type a company's name and get its website address back, using a very old, very simple lookup tool.

questions: using whois to find company websites
how does the company name lookup protocol work
why use whois instead of ldap or x500
what does a whois query return
subtitle: A simple way to find company websites by looking up company names

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew, the convention of guessing company websites from their names (e.g., www.xyz.com) stopped working because too many companies had legitimate claims to similar domain names.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes using WHOIS, one of the oldest Internet directory protocols, to match a company name against a database and return the company's website URL.
tldr.outcome: The approach trades simplicity for power: it works but requires maintaining accurate company databases and may return multiple matches. The idea was tested but never widely adopted, as search engines and DNS grew to fill the need differently.

today: RFC 2345 is Experimental and remains undeployed. Web search engines and DNS-based discovery became the dominant approaches instead, making this protocol unnecessary.

sections.title: The Top-Level Domain Problem
sections.content:
The Internet faced a naming challenge: as organizations multiplied, assuming that a company with a particular name would have a website at www.companyname.com became unreliable. Multiple legitimate organizations might have similar names or operate in different jurisdictions. The RFC identifies three distinct problems mixed together in industry discussions: domain administration policy, trademark ownership, and the information location problem. This RFC focuses on the third: how to locate the web pages for an entity when you know its name but not its domain name.

Previous proposals had suggested complex directory protocols like LDAP, WHOIS++, X.500, and RWHOIS, but none gained wide deployment. The hypothesis explored here is that simplicity might succeed where complexity failed.
sections.eli5: Companies have so many names in common that you cannot guess their website addresses. A simple lookup system might work better than fancy fancy directory systems.

sections.title: How the System Works
sections.content:
WHOIS is the Internet's oldest directory protocol, first published in 1982. The client simply opens a connection to port 43, sends a line of text containing a company name, and the server returns matching results. The RFC proposes adding a new use: queries send company names, and responses return one or more lines, each containing a URL, spaces, and a company name.

If a single match is found, the client automatically fetches that URL. If multiple matches are found, the user chooses from a list. The protocol allows two query variants: plain 7-bit ASCII (variation 0) and UTF-8 (variation 1). Servers match queries according to their own rules—the RFC deliberately does not specify how matching should work, leaving that to the server implementation.
sections.eli5: You type a company name into a very simple telephone call (like the oldest directory assistance), and the helper reads back the website address. Simple enough that almost anyone can do it.

sections.title: Query and Response Formats
sections.content:
A client query can be either a plain company name (equivalent to version 0) or a variation number prefixed with a slash and the name, such as 1/Company Name. For variation 0, all alphabetic text is case-insensitive. The server returns lines in the format: a URL, one or more spaces, and a company name. Lines are terminated with CR LF, following standard Internet conventions.

Servers may also return error messages in the form /// Not found or /// Variation not supported. The format is minimal by design: the RFC makes no claim about what the company name field should contain beyond display text for the user. It might be a name alone, a name with location and business type, or other information at the server's discretion.
sections.eli5: You send words in a very simple form, and you get back words in a simple form. No complicated structure that would confuse people.

sections.title: Why WHOIS over Richer Protocols
sections.content:
Critics asked why the RFC did not use more powerful directory protocols already standardized by the IETF. The authors gave several reasons: WHOIS is extremely simple, has a huge deployed base of clients and servers, and demonstrates whether a minimalist approach can work. If it proved too simple, evolution to richer protocols would be possible. More importantly, complex protocols had faced a chicken-and-egg problem: there was no agreement on a winner, and deployment was delayed by that choice.

The authors also noted that complex protocols require extensive configuration and training for casual users, which may deter adoption. A simpler approach allows the basic service to be offered inexpensively or free, while advanced features could be paid services. Maintaining a directory is fundamentally difficult; simplicity helps distribute that burden across multiple providers.
sections.eli5: Fancy systems with lots of options are hard to set up and hard to use. Something very simple is easier for everyone, even if it cannot do everything.
